Multitude
MūL-ti-tūd
n. (rendering Hebrew hāmōn and rōb, Greek ochlos and plēthos)
From Latin multitudo, from multus, many. The Hebrew hāmōn is onomatopoeic in its root sense — it means a murmur, a roar, the noise a great crowd makes — so that the Hebrew for multitude begins with the sound of one and only afterwards means the thing itself. Greek ochlos is the common crowd, the throng, and carries in the Gospels a distinct pathos: the ochlos is the mass of ordinary people, neither the rulers nor the disciples, pressed upon and unshepherded.

Biblical Definition

A multitude in Scripture is never treated as a moral authority, and the Bible's clearest statement on the subject cuts directly against the instinct of every crowd: “Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil; neither shalt thou speak in a cause to decline after many to wrest judgment” (Exo 23:2). Numbers do not make a thing right; the command anticipates that they will feel as though they do, and forbids the inference. Yet multitude is not a negative word. In counsel it is a positive good, because many advisers expose what one man cannot see: “Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14) — the same book that warns against following the crowd commends consulting many. The Gospels then give the word its most tender use. The Lord Jesus looks at the crowd and does not see a mob or a market: “But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd” (Mat 9:36). And the last vision shows what becomes of the multitudes He came for — not a manageable remnant but a company beyond counting: “a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes” (Rev 7:9). Scripture therefore refuses both the flattery of the crowd and the contempt of it.

Webster 1828 Definition

A great number of persons or things collectively; a crowd or throng; the mass of common people; and in Scripture the crowd Christ pitied as sheep without a shepherd, and the innumerable redeemed multitude before the throne.

expand to see more

MULTITUDE, n. 1. The state of being many; a great number, indefinitely.

2. A number collectively; the sum of many; as a multitude of counsellors. Prov. 11.

3. A great number of people assembled; a crowd; a throng.

4. The populace; the mass of men, without reference to rank or condition; the vulgar.

5. In Scripture, thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil. Exod. 23. A great multitude, which no man could number. Rev. 7.

Exodus 23:2 — "Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil; neither shalt thou speak in a cause to decline after many to wrest judgment:"

Proverbs 11:14 — "Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety."

Matthew 9:36 — "But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted , and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd."

Revelation 7:9 — "After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number , of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands;"

Modern Corruption

Majority sentiment is treated as the arbiter of truth and morality, so that a doctrine is judged by how many hold it and a practice justified by how widely it is accepted — the precise reasoning Exodus 23:2 forbids.

expand to see more

The characteristic error of a democratic age is to convert a description into a warrant: because most people now think a thing, the thing must be so. The reasoning is invisible because it feels like realism rather than argument, and it operates in the church as readily as outside it, wherever a doctrine is quietly retired on the ground that it has become a minority position. Exo 23:2 was given precisely against this reflex, and it was given first as a rule for courts — do not decline after many to wrest judgment — because the pressure of the crowd on a witness or a judge is the place where the reflex does its most concrete damage. Scripture's counter-examples are relentless: the whole congregation sided with the ten spies against Joshua and Caleb, and the whole multitude cried crucify him. Truth is not settled by counting.

The opposite corruption is an aristocratic contempt for ordinary people, which reads the Gospels' crowds as a fickle mob and concludes that the mass of men are beneath serious spiritual concern. The Lord's own response forbids it. He saw the multitudes and was moved with compassion, and the reason given is a pastoral diagnosis rather than a moral verdict: they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd. Their fickleness was the symptom of having no one to feed them. The principle to recover is that the crowd is neither an authority to be obeyed nor a rabble to be despised, but a field of shepherdless people for whom the appointed remedy is preachers — pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew hāmōn is a murmur, roar, or tumult, and hence a crowd; rōb is abundance or greatness of number. Greek ochlos is the common throng, and plēthos is a fulness or great number, whence the innumerable multitude of Revelation.

expand to see more

Hebrew hāmōn (H1995) — a noise, murmur, or roar; then the crowd that makes it; then abundance or great number.

Hebrew rōb (H7230) — multitude, abundance, greatness; in the multitude of counsellors there is safety (Pro 11:14).

Greek ochlos (G3793) — a throng or crowd, especially the common people as distinct from rulers; the word used of the multitudes Christ pitied.

Greek plēthos (G4128) — a fulness, great number, multitude; used of the heavenly host (Luk 2:13) and of the whole assembly of believers.

Greek ochlopoieō (G3792) — to gather a crowd, to raise a mob; used of the rabble stirred up against Paul at Thessalonica (Act 17:5).

Usage

"Of the crowd as no moral warrant: thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil (Exo 23:2)."

"Of many counsellors as safety: in the multitude of counsellors there is safety (Pro 11:14)."

"Of the innumerable redeemed: a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations (Rev 7:9)."
